item.title: Why Do Dogs Eat Grass?
item.description: Most dogs that eat grass are not doing anything dangerous or mysterious. Grass eating is common in dogs, and in most cases it is a normal scavenging or exploratory behavior rather than a sign of...

item.title: Why Do Messy Networks Sometimes Outlast Perfect Ones?
item.description: For decades scientists assumed that tidy, uniform systems are the most reliable. A new mathematical framework flips that idea on its head — a little well-placed variety can actually make a network tougher.

item.title: Could Fusion Energy Have a Secret Shortcut Around Its Biggest Hurdle?
item.description: For 70 years, scientists have tried to climb the fusion-energy mountain head-on. A new set of calculations suggests there may be a far easier pass around the side.

item.title: Can GPS-Free Satellites Navigate Space Using Only Their Neighbors?
item.description: A NASA experiment called FALCON shows spacecraft can work out their position in orbit by treating other satellites and space junk as floating landmarks — no GPS required.

item.title: Why Might the Human Family Tree Need a Big Rewrite?
item.description: A new paper argues that the three familiar groups of our ancient relatives — Homo, Australopithecus and Paranthropus — don't match real branches of the family tree, and that it may be time to merge them.

item.title: Why Is CERN Taking Apart Its Giant Atom Smasher?
item.description: The world's largest particle collider is being carefully opened up for the first time in nearly twenty years. The reason? New magnets that are about 40% stronger than the ones they replace.

item.title: Why Has a 100-Year-Old Mushroom Mystery Suddenly Grown So Complicated?
item.description: For more than a century, growers blamed one bacterium for the unsightly bruises on white button mushrooms. A new DNA study has found the culprit is not one germ but a whole crowd of them.

item.title: Why Does Quantum Weirdness Fade Away? Scientists Just Cleared One Big Suspect
item.description: Tiny particles can be in two states at once, yet everyday objects never do. A 62-day experiment buried under a mountain has ruled out one famous explanation for why the strange behaviour disappears.

item.title: Why Do Some New Skills Stick — and Could a Nerve in Your Neck Help?
item.description: Scientists in Japan found that gently stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice remember a new skill for longer — suggesting the body may quietly help the brain lock in what we learn.

item.title: Why Do Astronauts Get Constipated in Space — and What Can a Blood Test Show?
item.description: Blood samples from 52 astronauts hint that microgravity slows food through the gut, nudging bacteria to ferment protein instead of fiber.

item.title: Why Did Someone Bury a Perfect 400-Year-Old Pot and Never Come Back?
item.description: A small clay pot, still completely whole after four centuries underground, has left archaeologists in Florida with a wonderful mystery: why would anyone bury something perfectly usable and simply walk away?

item.title: Why Did Einstein Call It 'Spooky' — And What Did Scientists Just Catch at CERN?
item.description: Deep inside the world's biggest atom smasher, physicists have caught a famously 'spooky' quantum effect linking two fleeting particles — proving that nature's strangest rule holds even in some of the most violent...

item.title: Why Did a Rare Beetle That Rides on Bees Come Back to Wales After 60 Years?
item.description: A little beetle that hitches a lift on bees to raise its young has turned up breeding in Wales for the first time in six decades — and its comeback is a hopeful sign.

item.title: Why Did a 25-Year-Old Quantum Puzzle Finally Get Solved?
item.description: For a quarter of a century, physicists could measure one famous kind of quantum link — but not its equally important twin. A team in Japan has now cracked the other one, opening a fresh doorway to quantum teleportation.

item.title: Why Couldn't a 10-Year Experiment Pin Down Gravity's Most Famous Number?
item.description: Scientists spent a decade trying to measure the strength of gravity. When they finally opened a sealed envelope holding the answer, the number surprised them — and deepened one of physics' oldest mysteries.

item.title: Why Can't Viking Museums Let Go of the Warrior Myth?
item.description: Scandinavia's great museums hold some of the world's finest Viking treasures. A new study of their displays finds they still lean on an old, mostly made-up picture of Vikings as tall, sword-wielding warriors.

item.title: Why Are Wasps Moving Into Homes Built for Ants?
item.description: For 10 million years, tropical Macaranga trees have traded room and board to ants in exchange for bodyguard duty. Now scientists in Borneo have found predatory wasps moving in — and turning the ants' cosy chambers...

item.title: What Is the Quantum 'Energy Ladder' That Took 40 Years to Measure?
item.description: For four decades, physicists predicted that certain quantum systems should settle into energy steps at very particular spacings — like rungs on a ladder. Now a team at Caltech has finally measured those rungs...

item.title: What Is the 'Cheshire Cat's Grin' Hiding Inside a Superconductor?
item.description: When some metals get cold enough, electricity flows through them with zero resistance. Now physicists have caught a ghostly 'grin' left behind by that magic — a pattern of paired electrons that lingers even after the...

item.title: What Did a Long-Lost Memoir Reveal About a War of 1812 Soldier?
item.description: A forgotten autobiography, found in a library 3,700 miles from home, has rewritten the story of Shadrack Byfield — a British soldier who lost his arm in battle, designed his own replacement, and refused to be forgotten.

item.title: What Are the 4 Warning Signs That a Storm Is About to Strengthen?
item.description: A storm can look fierce from above yet still be going nowhere. After studying nearly 30 years of Hurricane Hunter radar, scientists have found four easy-to-spot clues that a disorganized storm is about to stand up —...

item.title: What Are \"In-Between\" Materials, and Why Could They Power the Future?
item.description: When chemists heat ingredients to make a new material, they usually watch only the start and the finish. A team in the UK peeked at the messy middle — and stumbled onto a hidden material that could help make clean...

item.title: What Are Fractons — the Strange Particles That Can Barely Move?
item.description: Imagine a particle so shy it refuses to budge on its own. Physicists have just brought fractons — oddities that barely move — a big step closer to being seen in a real material.

item.title: What Are Bethe Strings, the Quantum Knots Predicted Nearly a Century Ago?
item.description: Back in 1931, physicist Hans Bethe imagined particles that could cling together without any chemical glue — a kind of quantum knot that only works in one dimension. Almost a hundred years later, scientists in Austria...

item.title: How Does Your Name End Up on an Asteroid?
item.description: Two astronomers in Northern Ireland just learned that chunks of space roughly 11 km wide now carry their names. Here's how a rock drifting in the asteroid belt becomes a lasting honour.
